task_row_model.query: Why did Russia exit World War I after the 1917 revolutions, and what immediate territorial losses resulted from the peace settlement?

documents.content: Academic excerpt: The Bolshevik seizure of power in late 1917 brought an ideological priority to withdraw Russia from the imperialist war. Lenin and the new government issued a Decree on Peace calling for an immediate end to hostilities and “peace without annexations or indemnities.” This political directive drove Soviet negotiators to seek a rapid cessation of fighting even as front-line control was fragmented. The passage also notes continuities with earlier antiwar movements and references older debates over conscription and national mobilization under the Tsar, which are background context rather than proximate causes.
documents.reasoning_trace: Included the Bolshevik political priority and the Decree on Peace as the ideological/official reason for seeking immediate withdrawal; marked the background on prewar conscription as tangential noise.

documents.content: Journalistic report: By autumn 1917 the Russian army was unraveling. After failed offensives and political agitation, large-scale desertions and breakdowns in command made sustained operations impossible; soldiers frequently refused orders and units collapsed. Facing this operational collapse, the new government negotiated a truce on the Eastern Front in late 1917 — an armistice that halted major combat while diplomats met. The piece contrasts Eastern collapse with continued Western fighting and briefly defines armistice versus treaty, then cites some unrelated statistics about prewar troop levels and casualty estimates as illustrative background.
documents.reasoning_trace: Provides operational/military cause (desertions, command collapse) and the late-1917 armistice that paused fighting; distinguishes armistice vs treaty as noise and includes unrelated casualty statistics as tangential material.

documents.content: Reference entry: Negotiations culminated in the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, signed on 3 March 1918, which formalized Russia’s exit from World War I. Under the treaty Russia ceded control of several border regions: Poland, Finland, and the Baltic provinces (including Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia), and large parts of Ukraine to the Central Powers or their client states. The entry emphasizes that the treaty ended large-scale hostilities on the Eastern Front and allowed Bolshevik leaders to redeploy forces to internal rivals in the ensuing civil war. A final paragraph offers speculative historiography on whether the concessions were avoidable.
documents.reasoning_trace: Records the formal treaty date and enumerates the territorial cessions as the immediate consequences; notes the treaty's role in ending Eastern Front fighting and enabling redeployment for the civil war; historiographical speculation is marked as noise.

task_row_model.golden_answer: After the 1917 revolutions the Bolshevik government prioritized immediate withdrawal from the war (Decree on Peace) while the Russian army was already collapsing from desertion and command breakdown; an armistice halted fighting in late 1917 and the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (3 March 1918) formally ended Russia’s participation, ceding Poland, Finland, the Baltic provinces, and Ukraine to the Central Powers.
